lead: Photonic crystals are dielectric structures whose refractive index repeats in one, two or three dimensions. The repetition makes some wavelengths reflect strongly and prevents them from travelling through the crystal. That blocked range is the photonic band gap. Engineers use it to make compact mirrors, traps for light, sharp bends on a chip, and fibres that guide light in a hollow core. The same Bragg-reflection idea appears in thin-film coatings, but a photonic crystal extends it from a stack of layers to a full periodic lattice.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.4 for modes in a layered dielectric, and Chapter 1.8 for guided strips on a chip.

sections.h3: One-dimensional photonic crystal and Bragg reflection

blocks.text: A one-dimensional photonic crystal is a stack of alternating dielectric layers. Let a be the period, one full pair of layers, and n_eff be the average refractive index of that pair. Light travelling down the stack is partly reflected at every interface. When the reflected waves return in phase, they add. This Bragg condition gives a stop band: wavelengths near λB are reflected and cannot pass through a long stack.

blocks.where: λB is the first-order band-gap centre wavelength; n_eff is the average refractive index of one period; a is the period, one full layer pair.

blocks.text: The band gap is a range of wavelengths, not a single line. Its width and strength depend on the index contrast between the two materials. A high-contrast stack can reflect a wide band over a wide range of angles; such a design is called an omnidirectional reflector. A low-contrast stack gives a narrow band. In a fibre or chip, the same stack can be grown as thin films, etched as trenches, or written by lithography. The reflector works because the periodic medium has no propagating mode inside the gap.

items: Estimate n_eff from the layer indices.
Find the period a = λB/(2 n_eff).
Simulate or measure reflectance across the band.

blocks.text: A two-dimensional photonic crystal has a periodic lattice in a plane, for example a grid of air holes in silicon. A three-dimensional crystal repeats in all three axes, such as a stack of spheres or a woodpile structure. The band gap can block light along chosen directions. A defect breaks the period: remove one row of holes and the missing row becomes a line-defect waveguide. Remove a few holes and you make a microcavity that traps a wavelength for many cycles. These defects are the working parts of photonic-crystal chips.

Fabrication follows the same logic. Lithography and etching make 2D slabs and line defects. Self-assembled crystals form by letting spheres settle into an ordered lattice; holographic fabrication uses interfering laser beams to write a periodic pattern in photoresist. Each method trades precision against cost and area. A photonic crystal fibre uses a periodic pattern of air holes running along the fibre length to confine light in a core.

At block level, two special effects appear. Negative refraction bends a beam to the same side of the normal in a photonic crystal. Self-collimation lets a beam travel straight without a guiding core because the lattice makes the group velocity point along one axis. Both are useful for dense optical circuits, but they need careful design.

sections.h3: Photonic crystal fibre and practical limits

blocks.text: Photonic crystal fibre (PCF) is a glass fibre with a regular array of air holes along its length. In an index-guiding PCF, the solid core has a higher average index than the holey cladding, so total internal reflection still guides light. In a band-gap PCF, the cladding's periodic holes create a gap and a hollow core can guide light inside that gap. Hollow-core fibre can carry high power and has low material loss, but coupling and fabrication tolerances are tight.

A photonic crystal is not a magic low-loss material. Scattering from rough holes, imperfect period, and coupling from a normal fibre add loss. The useful band must overlap the source wavelength. For 1550 nm links, the period is set so λB sits near 1550 nm, often around 500 nm for n_eff near 1.5. The same design rule appears in thin-film filters, Bragg gratings, and laser mirrors. Plasmonics and metamaterials are related advanced topics beyond this unit.

examples.question: A one-dimensional photonic crystal is made from alternating layers with average refractive index n_eff = 1.5. The period is a = 500 nm, where one period is one full layer pair. Find the first-order band-gap centre wavelength in nanometres and in micrometres.
steps: Write the first-order Bragg condition: λB ≈ 2 n_eff a.
Substitute the data: n_eff = 1.5 and a = 500 nm.
examples.answer: The first-order band-gap centre is 1500 nm, or 1.5 μm.
examples.check:
n_eff = 1.5
a_nm = 500.0
lambda_nm = 2 * n_eff * a_nm
lambda_um = lambda_nm / 1000.0
print(lambda_nm)
print(lambda_um)

traps: The band gap is a range of wavelengths, not one exact wavelength. The centre λB is a label for the middle of the stop band.
The period a is one full layer pair. A single layer is not the period, even if the two layers have equal thickness.
Use n_eff, the average index of the period, in λB ≈ 2 n_eff a. Using only the high-index value shifts the predicted centre.
A 1D stack is not automatically an omnidirectional reflector. Wide-angle reflection needs high index contrast and careful layer design.
Do not mix the photonic band gap with the electronic band gap of a semiconductor. They are different gaps for different waves.

quiz.q: Define the photonic band gap in one sentence.
quiz.a: A photonic band gap is a range of wavelengths for which a periodic dielectric structure has no propagating mode, so light in that range is reflected or decays.

quiz.q: Why is the period a taken as one full layer pair in λB ≈ 2 n_eff a?
quiz.a: The Bragg condition repeats after two layers, one high-index and one low-index layer; a single layer is only half the period, so using it would halve the predicted wavelength.

quiz.q: A 1D photonic crystal has period a = 420 nm and average index n_eff = 1.45. Find the first-order band-gap centre.
Explain how removing one row of holes in a 2D photonic crystal makes a waveguide.
quiz.a: The missing row is a line defect; it breaks the periodic lattice and creates an allowed mode inside the band gap. Light cannot spread into the surrounding crystal, so it is guided along the defect.

quiz.q: Name two methods used to make 3D photonic crystals.
quiz.a: Self-assembly of spheres and holographic lithography with interfering laser beams.
A high-index-contrast 1D photonic crystal designed to reflect a band of wavelengths over a wide range of incidence angles.

quiz.q: A 1D photonic crystal must have its first-order gap at 1550 nm with n_eff = 1.5. Find the period a.
Why does a photonic band gap not guarantee a low-loss fibre?
quiz.a: The gap only blocks propagation in the periodic region. Rough holes, period errors, coupling loss, and a band that does not overlap the source still add loss; a hollow-core fibre also needs a robust single-mode design.

beyond: Not for the exam. Silicon photonics uses photonic-crystal cavities to make tiny modulators and filters on a chip. Hollow-core photonic-band-gap fibre is being developed for low-latency links and high-power beam delivery. Researchers also study topological photonic crystals, which guide light along edges that are robust to disorder.
